title: Sharp finite-market prophet inequalities for a single threshold
shortTitle: One price, n buyers: exact guarantees
oneLine: Exact worst-case guarantees of one fixed price or threshold at every market size, for buyers with different value distributions arriving in random order, and a proof of the Arnosti-Ma stockout conjecture.
abstract: A seller with k identical items faces n buyers who arrive in random order with independent, possibly different value distributions, posts one fixed price and sells to the first k buyers who will pay it; the benchmark is a prophet who keeps the best l values. This candidate gives the exact worst-case fraction of the prophet's value, at every finite market size n > max(k, l), for the best distribution-aware threshold, for a threshold calibrated to a stockout probability and for one calibrated to an expected utilisation, together with the identical-law values and the boundary cases. Two binomial expectations determine every answer. The utilisation rule at its best finite target loses nothing against full knowledge of the distributions; the stockout rule is strictly worse for k ≥ 2, but only by an amount of exact order 1/n², about 0.030/n² for two items; identical laws are easier by an amount of order 1/n, about 0.18/n for two items. With three buyers and two items the guarantees are 79.1%, 78.7% at the best stockout target, and 85.2% for identical laws. Over all market sizes the stockout target proposed by Arnosti and Ma attains their constant 1 − e^{−k}k^k/k! for every k, which proves their conjecture; as the paper records, their own Lemma 1 combined with the crossing lemma already yields it. For unequal capacities the same corollary answers a question of Molina, Gast, Loiseau and Perchet for static thresholds. The method compares counts at a common stockout probability: the distribution functions cross exactly once. A single instance with one rare, very valuable buyer defeats every threshold at once. Limits: one anonymous fixed threshold, independent values, random order (or stated mixtures), worst-case values. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 2.1 (proof, main): for n > max(k, l) and independent heterogeneous values in random order, the fixed-stockout value is S(q) = min{U_n(p_n(q)), (l/k)A_{n-1}(p_{n-1}(q))}; the all-static value C solves U_{n-1}(p) = (l/k)A_{n-1}(p); the identical-law value is U_n(l/n). One instance defeats every threshold and every randomisation over thresholds.
Lemma 2.2 (proof): a Bernoulli sum and a binomial or Poisson count with the same stockout probability have distribution functions that cross exactly once, at k − 1.

Proposition 2.4 (proof): a threshold calibrated to the utilisation target C attains the distribution-aware value C at every n; Propositions 2.5 and 2.6 settle the boundary cases and the identical-law stockout curve.

Corollary 3.1 (proof, main): over all market sizes the stockout target P(Pois(k) ≥ k) attains 1 − e^{−k}k^k/k! for every k, proving the Arnosti-Ma conjecture; for unequal capacities the value (1/k)Σ_j P(Pois(l) ≥ j) holds for heterogeneous values, answering the question of Molina et al. for static thresholds.

Corollaries 3.2 and 3.3 (proof): the stockout rule loses an amount of exact order 1/n² (about 0.030/n² for k = l = 2); heterogeneity costs an amount of order 1/n, strictly positive at every n (about 0.18/n for k = l = 2). Example: n = 3, k = l = 2 gives 79.1%, 78.7% and 85.2%.

narration:
This is an audio briefing from Evidence Press on a research candidate about what one fixed price can guarantee when buyers arrive one at a time.

Picture a seller with a few identical items and a line of buyers who turn up in random order. Each buyer's value comes from a known distribution, and buyers can differ. The seller posts one price, never changes it, and sells to the first buyers who will pay it. The same rule describes one hiring bar for a few posts. The yardstick is a prophet who sees every value in advance and keeps the best ones.

One price is simple and fair, and it can be tuned from data, for example by adjusting it until the stock sells out a chosen share of the time. For very large markets, Arnosti and Ma found the best guarantee: about sixty-three percent with one item and seventy-three percent with two items. They conjectured that tuning the price to a particular sell-out probability also achieves it.

This paper gives the exact worst-case guarantee at every market size, for buyers who may differ, and proves that conjecture for any number of items. With three buyers and two items, the best fixed price guarantees seventy-nine point one percent, the best sell-out target guarantees seventy-eight point seven percent, and if every buyer's value has the same distribution, the guarantee rises to eighty-five point two percent. In general, tuning the average share of stock sold loses nothing, the sell-out target loses only a tiny amount, and differences between buyers cost a little more.

The key idea compares the number of buyers who clear the price with a simple count that sells out equally often: their distribution curves cross exactly once. A market of ordinary buyers plus one rare, very valuable buyer defeats every possible price at once, so the guarantees cannot be improved. As the paper says, Arnosti and Ma's own lemma combined with this crossing argument already settles their conjecture.

The limits are clear: one anonymous fixed price, independent values and random arrival order, and these are worst cases, so typical markets do better.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and computer calculations rather than by peer review, and this briefing uses a synthetic voice that is not additional evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Anonymous (2026), Asymptotic i.i.d. prophet inequalities: fixed-capacity limits and certified two-unit bounds. Evidence Press (Zenodo). Adaptive policies for identically distributed values in the large-market limit; cited for the gap between static and adaptive rules.

Arnosti and Ma (2023), Tight Guarantees for Static Threshold Policies in the Prophet Secretary Problem. Operations Research. The large-market constant, the utilisation rule, the two-coefficient bound (Lemma 1) and the stockout conjecture (Section 5.2), proved here for every market size.
Chawla, Devanur and Lykouris (2024), Static Pricing for Multi-unit Prophet Inequalities. Operations Research. The static-pricing constant under adversarial arrival order.
Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim and Singla (2018), Prophet Secretary for Combinatorial Auctions and Matroids. Proceedings of SODA 2018. The single-item rule, the case k = 1 of the stockout conjecture.

Jiang, Ma and Zhang (2026), Tightness Without Counterexamples: A New Approach and New Results for Prophet Inequalities. Mathematics of Operations Research. Exact finite values for identical laws and for adversarial order.

Molina, Gast, Loiseau and Perchet (2025), Prophet Inequalities: Competing with the Top ℓ Items is Easy. Proceedings of SODA 2025. The unequal-capacity constant for identical laws and the question, answered here for static thresholds.
Yu (2010), Relative log-concavity and a pair of triangle inequalities. Bernoulli. Relative log-concavity of Bernoulli sums, used in the crossing lemma.
